q-28194.name: Question 1
q-28194.problem:
Given that $(x+1)$ is a factor of $f(x)=-{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}-4x-2,$ which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

(*Note: Figures not drawn to scale*)
q-28194.worked_solution:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that $(x+1)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so $(x+1)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder. To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x+1)$ using synthetic division:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ -1 & -1 & -3 & -4 & -2 \\  &  & 1 & 2 & 2 \\  & -1 & -2 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{f(x)}{x+1} & =-{x}^{2}-2x-2 \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2x+2),\end{aligned}
$$

which means that

$$
f(x)=-(x+1)({x}^{2}+2x+2).
$$

The equation is now fully factored. Note that the discriminant of ${x}^{2}+2x+2=0$ is 

$$
D={2}^{2}-4(1)(2)=-4<0,
$$

which implies that the quadratic factor has no real roots. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that $f(x)$ has a single root at $x=-1.$ 

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
y=-(0)^{3}-3(0)^{2}-4(0)-2=-2
$$

So, the curve:

- has a $y$-intercept at $(0,-2),$

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=-1,$ and

- has no more $x$-intercepts.

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the graph has an $\text{S}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

q-38949.problem:
Given that $(x+1)$ is a factor of $f(x)={x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+3x+3,$ which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

(*Note: Figures not drawn to scale*)
q-38949.worked_solution:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that $(x+1)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so $(x+1)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder. To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x+1)$ using synthetic division:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ -1 & 1 & 1 & 3 & 3 \\  &  & -1 & 0 & -3 \\  & 1 & 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{f(x)}{x+1}={x}^{2}+3
$$

which means that

$$
f(x)=(x+1)({x}^{2}+3).
$$

The equation is now fully factored. Note that the discriminant of ${x}^{2}+3=0$ is 

$$
D={0}^{2}-4(1)(3)=-12<0,
$$

which implies that the quadratic factor has no real roots. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that $f(x)$ has a single root at $x=-1.$ 

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={0}^{3}+{0}^{2}+3(0)+3=3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the curve:

- has a $y$-intercept at $(0,3),$

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=-1,$ and

- has no more $x$-intercepts.

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted $\text{S}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

$$

$$

which implies that the quadratic factor has no real roots. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that $f(x)$ has a single root at $x=0.$ 

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

y=-{0}^{3}-2(0)^{2}-4(0)=0

- has a $y$-intercept at $(0,0),$
